newsitem.title: JORDAN: British land speed record hopes flooded in desert.
newsitem.headline: British land speed record hopes flooded in desert.

text.p: Flash floods in Jordan's southern deserts have washed away British dreams of breaking the world land speed record this year.

Members of the Thrust Supersonic team testing their 9.5 tonne jet-powered car on the mud-flats of al-Jafr, 125 miles (200 km) south of Amman, said on Wednesday the heaviest rains in five years had turned their parched desert track into a lake.

"We are going to have to stop for the year. This really is extreme weather, and it's beaten us," said Andrew Noble, whose brother Richard was leading the assault on his own world record of 633.47 mph (1,019.44 kph), set in 1983.

The flash floods, which killed three people and caused serious damage to roads and houses in southern Jordan, swept onto the desert floor on Tuesday from mountain ranges around Jordan's ancient Nabatean city of Petra, Noble said.

He said the team of 26 engineers, designers and assistants managed to load up the giant aluminium and carbon fibre car onto a truck on Tuesday and take it to the safety of a military base before they were cut off by floodwaters.
"The whole area is now in about three to four inches (10 cm) of water," Noble told Reuters by phone from al-Jafr. "It's the first time the lake has been flooded since 1991."

The team were originally drawn to al-Jafr, where scenes from Lawrence of Arabia were filmed, because they thought its bone-dry weather would guarantee a chance to drive Thrust SSC into the record books.

They had planned to reach 650 mph (1,040 kph) in Jordan in preparation for an even more ambitious target next year -- smashing the sound barrier (about 750 mph/1,200 kph) in the deserts of Nevada in the United States.
But the car, powered by twin jet engines from a Phantom warplane and designed to reach up to 850 mph (1,360 kph), never got above a sedate 300 mph (480 kph).

"We'll work on the car over the winter and we're making plans to come back to Jordan next year," Noble said, adding they had identified a 14.2 mile (22.7 km) stretch of desert that could be long enough for the car to hit supersonic speed.
Noble's team, who expect to fly back to Britain next week, are not the only speed merchants facing a frustrated winter.

Earlier this month their main rival, American Craig Breedlove, had to call off his own challenge at the world record when his car, the Spirit of America, was damaged in a high speed accident in the Black Rock desert of Nevada in the United States.
Noble scouted around Jordan for other sites that could meet the team's needs, but failed to a long enough stretch of desert that escaped the floods.

One possible strip, near the border with Iraq, turned out to be "an excellent surface" but at just five miles (eight km) long, it was far too short for the car to reach its top speeds and slow down again, even with parachute brakes.
